e.etymology: From French Rene, from the Late Latin name Renatus (born again), which early Christians used for spiritual rebirth in baptism. In the US it is mostly a boys' name in Hispanic families; Renee is the feminine form.
namesakes: Rene Descartes (French philosopher, I think therefore I am)
Rene Russo (actress in The Thomas Crown Affair)
Rene Magritte (Belgian surrealist painter)

e.etymology: The English adjective for loud, unruly behavior, an Americanism first recorded in the early 1800s. It reached first-name use by way of cowboy and rodeo culture and as a long-standing nickname.
namesakes: Rowdy Yates (Clint Eastwood's cowboy on Rawhide)
Rowdy Gaines (Olympic champion swimmer and broadcaster)
e.note: It is also the everyday word for loud and unruly, so the name sets an expectation and invites jokes.

e.etymology: From Hebrew me'ir (one who gives light, illuminates), from or (light). The 2nd-century sage Rabbi Meir made it a lasting Jewish name; Meyer and Mayer are its Yiddish-influenced forms.

assoc.t: Golda Meir, prime minister of Israel

e.etymology: An Italian name of Germanic origin, a short form of names beginning with ald (old) and, in some cases, adal (noble). It is also common in Latin America.
namesakes: Aldo Leopold (conservationist, author of A Sand County Almanac)
Aldo Raine (Brad Pitt's lieutenant in Inglourious Basterds)

e.etymology: From French Renee, the feminine of Rene, from the Late Latin name Renata (born again), which early Christians linked to spiritual rebirth in baptism.
namesakes: Renee Zellweger (Oscar-winning actress, Bridget Jones's Diary)
Renee Fleming (opera soprano)
Renee Rapp (singer and Mean Girls actress)

e.etymology: From Biblical Hebrew Bo'az, of uncertain meaning but probably related to oz (might, strength). Boaz is the kind landowner who marries Ruth and becomes King David's great-grandfather.
namesakes: Boaz (husband of Ruth in the Book of Ruth)

e.etymology: A spelling variant of Melanie, from Latin Melania, from Greek melas (black, dark). This spelling is used mostly in Spanish-speaking families.
A respelling of Cooper, an English occupational surname for someone who made and repaired wooden barrels and casks.

e.meaning: Irish form of Catherine, traditionally pure
e.etymology: An Anglicized form of Irish Caitlin, which came from Old French Cateline, a form of Catherine. Catherine goes back to Greek Aikaterine, whose meaning is debated but was long linked to katharos (pure).
namesakes: Kathleen Turner (actress in Romancing the Stone)
Kathleen Kennedy (producer of Star Wars and Jurassic Park films)

e.etymology: From the Basque word ainara (swallow), a variant of enara. It is a modern Basque given name that has spread through the Spanish-speaking world.
A recent American coinage with no documented source. It shares its sounds with Jasiah, Josiah and Kasai.
From an English occupational surname for someone who covered roofs with straw or reeds, from Old English theccan (to cover).
e.note: Many people think first of Margaret Thatcher, a divisive figure, especially in Britain and Ireland.

e.etymology: A Japanese girls' name whose meaning depends on the characters used to write it. In the US it sits beside the better-known Kiyomi, most often written with the characters for pure and beauty.

e.meaning: short form of Alexandra, defender of men
e.etymology: A short form of Alexandra and, less often, Cassandra, taken into English from Italian. Alexandra is the feminine of Alexander, from Greek words for defend and man.
namesakes: Sandra Bullock (actress in Speed and The Blind Side)
Sandra Day O'Connor (first woman on the US Supreme Court)
Sandra Oh (actress in Grey's Anatomy and Killing Eve)

e.etymology: From the River Kelvin in Glasgow, whose Gaelic name may mean narrow water. Physicist William Thomson took the title Lord Kelvin in 1892, and the given name followed.

assoc.t: kelvin, the scientific unit of temperature

e.meaning: pet form of Lawrence, from Laurentum
e.etymology: A pet form of Lawrence and Laurence, from Latin Laurentius (man from Laurentum, a town near Rome). It was popular as a given name in its own right in the US in the 1940s and 1950s.
namesakes: Larry Bird (Boston Celtics legend)
Larry David (creator of Curb Your Enthusiasm)
Larry King (talk show host)

e.etymology: From Greek Hagne, from hagnos (pure, chaste). Saint Agnes, a young Roman martyr, made it one of the most common names of medieval Europe; her emblem is a lamb, from Latin agnus.
namesakes: Agnes Moorehead (Endora on Bewitched)
Agnes (the unicorn-loving youngest girl in Despicable Me)
Saint Agnes of Rome (early Christian martyr)

assoc.t: Agnes, the littlest girl in Despicable Me

e.etymology: The French form of Lucian, from Latin Lucianus, a derivative of the Roman name Lucius, from lux (light).
The Latin form of Greek Demetrios, meaning belonging to Demeter, the goddess of grain and the harvest, whose own name is read as earth mother. Several ancient kings and an early saint bore it.
namesakes: Demetrius (suitor in A Midsummer Night's Dream)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Qayin. Genesis ties it to the verb qanah (to acquire), while the word itself suggests a smith or craftsman. Modern use also draws on the surnames Cain and Kane.
namesakes: Cain (son of Adam and Eve, who killed his brother Abel)

assoc.t: the Bible's first murderer, who killed his brother Abel

e.note: In Genesis Cain murders his brother Abel; many people will make that connection first.

e.meaning: smile; often written as blessed beauty
e.etymology: A Japanese girls' name from the stem of the verb emu (to smile, to bloom), commonly written with characters such as blessing and beauty. In the US it also serves as a short form of Emily and Emilia.
From Medieval Latin Clarissa, built on Clara, from clarus (clear, bright), and tied to the order of Saint Clare of Assisi. Samuel Richardson's 1748 novel Clarissa popularized it in English.
namesakes: Clarissa Darling (teen lead of Clarissa Explains It All)
Clarissa Dalloway (heroine of Virginia Woolf's Mrs Dalloway)

assoc.t: teen lead of Nickelodeon's Clarissa Explains It All

e.etymology: The Scandinavian spelling of Christian, from Latin Christianus (follower of Christ), from Greek Christos (the anointed one). It has been recorded in Sweden since 1291.
The Spanish form of Ulysses, from Latin Ulixes, the Roman name for Odysseus, the wandering hero of Homer's Odyssey. The meaning of the Greek name is not known for certain.
James spelled backward, a coinage that arose in African American families. James itself goes back through Latin Iacomus to the Hebrew name Yaakov (Jacob).
From Sanskrit arya (noble, honorable). The doubled a marks the long first vowel of the Indian name, which is given to both girls and boys; Arya is the more common spelling.

assoc.t: Arya Stark of Game of Thrones, usually spelled Arya

e.meaning: of the Roman Claudius family, from claudus, lame
e.etymology: The feminine of Claudius, the name of a great Roman family that the Romans themselves linked to claudus (lame). It has been used in English since the 16th century.
namesakes: Claudia Schiffer (German supermodel)
Claudia Kishi (artist of The Baby-Sitters Club)
Claudia Sheinbaum (president of Mexico)

e.etymology: A modern American combination of Mae and the -lynn ending, in the pattern of Raelynn and Jaelynn. Mae is a spelling of May, a pet form of Mary and Margaret.
The English word, from Old English hunig, for the sweet food made by bees and a long-standing term of endearment. It began as an affectionate nickname and is now given as a name in its own right.
namesakes: Honey Ryder (Ursula Andress's Bond girl in Dr. No)

assoc.t: everyday term of endearment, like sweetie
honey, the sweet food made by bees

e.note: Honey is what many people call a partner, a child or a stranger, so she will hear it used for everyone.

e.etymology: A Japanese name most often written with kiyo (pure, clean) and mi (beautiful); another spelling uses the character for holy. In Japan it is given mainly to girls.
From an English surname that began as a nickname for someone of noble birth or manners, from Old French genterie. Gentry is still the English word for the landed upper class.
A respelling of Amira, from Arabic amira (princess), the feminine of amir (prince, commander).
